To analyze model decision boundaries, we apply a tripartite Explainable AI (xAI) framework using SHAP. Our analysis reveals three key phenomena: First, detectors often rely on a "Call-to-Action" syndrome inherent to instruction-tuned LLMs rather than generic machine text. Second, we observe a "Specificity Bias," where LLMs successfully bypass detection by hallucinating specific named entities and mimicking conversational imperfection. Finally, we illustrate the "Wikipedia Paradox," wherein formal, objective human writing is frequently misclassified as AI due to its low statistical burstiness. These findings demonstrate that purely statistical detection paradigms face systematic limitations in highly structured human domains, emphasizing the critical need for semantically-aware, interpretable detection architectures.
item.dc:creator: Nico Morloher, Johannes Reschke, Mohamed Mady

item.title: MultiInpaintCOCO: Fine-Grained Visual Understanding in Multiple Languages
item.description: arXiv:2611.03309v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Previous research shows that vision-language (VL) models struggle to understand fine-grained image details and tend to focus on the overall layout. Moreover, any weakness in English tends to be further amplified in the multilingual setting. To study that, we extend InpaintCOCO, an English dataset focused on fine-grained visual details, to 13 typologically diverse languages across five language families, creating MultiInpaintCOCO - a new multilingual benchmark of 953 minimal-pair examples. We further test several state-of-the-art models in multilingual multimodal retrieval, considering both light VL CLIP-like encoders and large language models. Our results show that performance degrades substantially for lower-resource languages, with the strongest predictor being the data resources available for the languages rather than typological similarity to English. In cross-lingual retrieval, most models exhibit a systematic bias toward English: when given a correct caption in a non-English language and an incorrect one in English, models preferentially select the English caption. This bias varies considerably across architectures. Among the tested models, Gemma 3 shows the strongest English preference while Qwen 3 is the least biased, despite both reaching similar monolingual accuracy across languages. The code is available at https://github.com/ufal/multi-inpaint-coco.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 6th Workshop on Multilingual Representation Learning (MRL 2026), pages 560-585
item.dc:creator: Andrei-Alexandru Manea, Jind\v{r}ich Libovick\'y, Philipp J. R\"osch

item.title: Steering with Multilingual Lexicons for Sentiment Control in Low-Resource Languages
item.description: arXiv:2611.03317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation steering offers a lightweight mechanism for controlling model behavior, but existing methods depend on sentence-level contrastive data that is unavailable for most of the world's languages. We show that multilingual sentiment lexicons are a viable substitute across three model families: aggregated multilingual lexicons outperform English-derived steering vectors for mid- and low-resource languages, while monolingual lexicons remain stronger for languages a model has specialized in during pre-training. The steering efficacy is mechanistically dictated by both representational density and pre-training priors. Large-magnitude English vectors overwhelm the compact representations of low-resource languages, causing "linguistic collapse." This fragility is mitigated by the norm-dampening of multilingual aggregation. Architectural biases, including bilingual specialization penalty and latent numerical rigidity, also heavily constrain cross-lingual steering responsiveness. Ultimately, our work establishes lexicons as a practical steering signal and offers a comprehensive mechanistic account of cross-lingual steering dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Lucinda Laurent, Muhammad Dehan Al Kautsar, Alfan Farizki Wicaksono, Fajri Koto

item.title: IdeaTaste: Do LLMs Share the Research Taste of Human Researchers?
item.description: arXiv:2611.03424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Research taste, the judgment of what to read, which problems to pursue, and which methods to try, increasingly shapes the work of AI scientists, yet it remains far less understood than their ability to execute research. We introduce IdeaTaste, a benchmark that scores an LLM by how closely the research proposals it writes from a literature snapshot frozen at 2025 match the work the same communities published in 2026. Our experiments span six contemporary language models and four research areas from established to emerging fields, covering more than 90{,}000 proposals in total. LLM agents fall well short of human communities in both the literature they cite and the ideas they state, reaching about 26\% of the human level on citation matching and only 18\% on idea matching. Their populations can cite as diversely as a community and take up its tasks and methods, yet rarely arrive at the concrete approaches and research plans it pursues. Neither richer field context nor larger populations substantially close this gap. In blinded expert review, AI proposals trail the 2026 papers least in presentation and most in expected success, echoing their gap in concrete approaches, and those whose ideas no human paper shares fare worst, suggesting weaker directions rather than overlooked opportunities. These results indicate that the main bottleneck in AI research taste lies less in finding the directions a community works on than in turning them into the concrete approaches it goes on to pursue. We release IdeaTaste as an open, continuously updated leaderboard (https://cxcscmu.github.io/IdeaTaste) that benchmarks contemporary AI proposals against future publication cycles.
item.dc:creator: Shanshan Zhong, Chen Xu, Jingjie Ning, Zhengzhong Liu, Aviral Kumar, Chenyan Xiong

item.title: VIAS: Value-Isolating Activation Steering for Multi-Value Alignment and Compliance for Organisations
item.description: arXiv:2611.03518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organisations increasingly deploy large language model agents that must follow organisational values. We check whether activation steering, which adds vectors to a model's internal activations during generation without changing its weights, can improve compliance beyond prompting alone. Since most scenarios involve several values at once, we focus on multi-value steering. A simple way to build these vectors is to contrast responses that follow all values relevant to a scenario with responses that violate them. However, this gives nearly identical vectors for different values: they capture a general compliance signal rather than individual values, which limits their use when combining several values. We propose Value-Isolating Activation Steering (VIAS), which contrasts responses to the same scenario under two prompts, one listing all relevant values and one omitting a single target value. We keep a pair only if the target value changes from compliant to non-compliant and both responses still meet a minimum compliance level on the other values. We evaluate VIAS on PROTECT, a workplace compliance dataset where each scenario is tagged with relevant values from a 21-value taxonomy. VIAS reduces overlap between value vectors, making them better suited for multi-value steering, although this alone does not lead to independent control over each value. Combined with prompting, VIAS complies with every tagged value on 69.6% of scenarios for Qwen2.5-7B, 75.2% for Mistral-7B, and 72.6% for Phi-3.5-mini, outperforming prompting alone for all three models.
item.dc:creator: Avni Mittal, Avinash Anand, Dikshant Kukreja, Erik Cambria, Rajiv Ratn Shah, Sandipan Dandapat

item.title: Can LLM Agents Be Forward-Deployed Engineers? Requirement Discovery and Delivery for Enterprise Text-to-SQL
item.description: arXiv:2611.03551v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM coding agents can increasingly automate model post-training, but whether they can act as forward-deployed engineer (FDE) agents, discovering customer requirements and turning them into deployment decisions, remains unclear. We study this on a real enterprise text-to-SQL engagement: a simulated customer, grounded in the real use case's requirements, starts with an ambiguous request. An agent must discover acceptance criteria, data permissions, and hardware constraints in the discovery phase, then plan and execute a post-training recipe in the delivery phase. Across 15 models, the strongest discover over 80% of withheld requirements and open-weight models discover 40-50%; in the delivery phase, only 25% of runs across eight coding-agent configurations pass all acceptance criteria. We identify four bottlenecks in this engagement: (1) incomplete discovery, with 40% of withheld requirements missing or misrepresented; (2) unreliable execution; (3) underused compute budgets and a lack of systematic comparisons across base models and post-training methods; and (4) benchmark accuracy does not guarantee production readiness. We suggest human review of discovered requirements, monitoring of the agent's plan during execution, and an explicit experiment-environment specification covering hardware, budget scope, and production checks.
item.dc:creator: Marianne Menglin Liu, Rongguang Wang, Zheng Wang, Yewen Wang, Leonid Boytsov, Tao Sheng, Sujith Ravi, Dan Roth

item.title: VeriHarm-Bench: Measuring Harmful Success in LLM Coding Agents Verifiably
item.description: arXiv:2611.03575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly operate with shell access, allowing them to write scripts, move files, alter permissions, and modify system configurations. However, an agent may achieve a user's goal while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data, in response to benign inputs without explicit jailbreaking. This failure mode is particularly important because apparent task success may reassure users that an agent behaved correctly, causing harmful side effects to go unnoticed. We call this harmful success: the agent successfully completes the intended benign task while simultaneously causing unintended harm. Despite its importance, harmful success is difficult to measure because conventional task-success metrics overlook harmful behaviors, while existing safety evaluations are often designed solely to assess harmful outcomes. We introduce VeriHarm, an automatic framework for constructing programmatically verifiable benchmarks that directly measure harmful success. VeriHarm minimally perturbs coding tasks to elicit unintended harmful behavior while maintaining the benignity of the task and preserving the original task objective. It then synthesizes executable harm tests that, together with the original task-correctness tests, evaluate both task accuracy and harmful outcomes. Frontier agents, including GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, achieve an average task accuracy of 95% on our curated VeriHarm-Bench, yet still struggle to complete tasks safely: their safe success rate, the fraction of tasks completed successfully without triggering the designated harm, averages only 37%. These results suggest that successful task completion can frequently coexist with unintended harm, and that task-success metrics alone may substantially understate the potential safety risks of coding agents.
item.dc:creator: Wei-Lin Chen, Zhepei Wei, Xinyu Zhu, Yu-Min Tseng, Tzu-Han Lin, Yu Meng

item.title: NitiBench+: A Temporal Thai Legal Question Answering Benchmark Across 17 Domains
item.description: arXiv:2611.03576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Law changes over time. A court decides a case under the law in force on that day, and legal QA benchmarks grade answers against today's law. We checked 156,650 decisions of four Thai courts. Up to 67% of them cite law that has since been amended or repealed. We introduce NitiBench+, the sequel of our NitiBench, a Thai legal QA benchmark with 1,670 items across 17 domains, built from decisions of three courts. For each cited section it holds both the text in force on the decision date and the current text, and its retrieval corpus holds every dated version of every Thai statute section. Answers are graded on the Thai Bar Council rubric, the Bar-standard score, and on the overlap between the cited sections and the court's. The report has two parts. Part I measures the cost of the wrong text on 13 open-weight models. Reading the current text of amended law drops the Bar-standard score by 0.25 and missing repealed law drops it by 0.79. The penalty comes from rule changes, 0.45 on the 428 rule-changed items and none on the 331 wording-only items, and Citation F1 does not see it. The text in force is the fair setting. Part II benchmarks today's models on that setting. A public leaderboard ranks 26 models on a held-out test split of 500 items stratified by domain, with a validation split of the same shape released for public use, from memory alone, with the court's sections provided, and as a retrieval agent over the law in force, with the cost per item and the hallucinated citations. The best model scores 7.78 out of 10 and the best open-weight model 6.39. Without a search tool only five open-weight models recall any Thai law, and with it twenty of the 26 models gain and six lose. Leaderboard will take new models as they are released. Legal benchmarks must track dates, and on the right text today's models still leave a wide gap on Thai law.
item.dc:creator: Pawitsapak Akarajaradwong, Sarana Nutanong, Chompakorn Chaksangchaichot

item.title: ufakzeka-kulak: Building and Evaluating a 31.6M-Parameter Turkish Speech Recognizer from Scratch
item.description: arXiv:2611.03605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: ufakzeka-kulak is an open Turkish speech-to-text model of 31.6M parameters, a FastConformer encoder with a token-and-duration transducer (TDT) and a CTC head, trained from scratch and released under Apache-2.0. It writes cased, punctuated Turkish with numbers as words. Its 4,977 training hours come from sources whose licences allow commercial use; 281 hours are human-transcribed, and for the other 4,696 the training text is an uploader subtitle or a machine transcript, kept only where a second, independent reading of the audio agrees with it. The recipe, checkpoint, labelling and export choices were made on development data, and the test sets were scored once, in a release gate fixed before training. With greedy TDT decoding the normalised word error rate (WER) is 0.0921 (95 percent interval 0.0792 to 0.1055) on FLEURS Turkish test and 0.0916 (0.0873 to 0.0958) on Common Voice 27.0 Turkish test, lower than Whisper base and Whisper small on both sets with paired intervals wholly below zero; Whisper large-v3 (greedy) scores 0.0604 and 0.0767. On conversational speech the WER is 0.3807. We also report punctuation and casing, degraded audio, and how closely each shipped export reproduces the trained model.
item.dc:creator: Sait Furkan Teke (ufak AI)

item.title: Tracing the Scientific Discovery Capacity of LLMs to Their Training Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.03617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show growing promise for scientific discovery, yet basic questions remain about what enables reliable discovery. How can we trace the scientific discovery capacity of LLMs to their training data? We study this question as one of missing probability mass and develop a theoretical account in which monofacts-the facts observed once during training-set the discovery capacity. In materials science and regulatory genomics, we directly manipulate monofact rates in training sets and find that more monofacts consistently yield more discoveries across two open-weight model families, sampling strategies, and reasoning budgets. Further experiments show the relationship cannot be explained by training-set diversity alone and can transfer across scientific domains when paired with in-domain data. Together, our results identify monofact rate in training data as a key factor governing discoveries in language models.
item.dc:creator: Arda Uzunoglu, Mahler Revsine, Michael Schatz, Benjamin Van Durme, Mehrdad Farajtabar, Daniel Khashabi, Eric Nalisnick

item.title: Total Cost of Agency: Exact Attribution of Memory Injection Cost in Multi-Agent LLM Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2609.23790v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Every node in a multi-agent large language model (LLM) workflow retrieves context from memory and injects it into its prompt, where those injected tokens are billed as input tokens at the same per-token price as the system prompt and the user query. Production observability tools report total token cost but do not separate the tokens a node generates from the tokens it is handed, so this component of the bill is invisible to the teams paying it. We introduce the Total Cost of Agency (TCA), a decomposition of multi-agent workflow cost into base prompt, inference, memory injection, miss penalty and context-accumulation components, and an exact attribution method: a two-pass, non-billable token count that measures injected tokens directly rather than estimating them from word-count proxies. On a 200-task enterprise benchmark executed against real model APIs, memory injection accounts for 13.6 percent of the variable cost a compile-time optimizer can act on, about 12 percent of the full billed cost, and its share rises from a structural zero at workflow depth one to 27.6 percent at depth six. Injected tokens grow linearly with depth over the measured range (R^2 = 0.9974, depths two through six); a quadratic fit yields a negative leading coefficient, so the data do not exhibit convex growth at these depths. We show the component is controllable at fixed model tier: reducing the retrieval window capacity from 32 to 2 entries lowers injected tokens by 28.7 percent with an accuracy change within seed-level variation. We report in full that our graph-rewriting transforms are approximately cost-neutral in isolation, that two of the five decomposition terms are zero by construction in this harness, and that total workflow cost is dominated by model tier assignment, which we hold fixed and treat as prior work. Prompt caching is not evaluated; all figures are for the uncached case.
item.dc:creator: Vivek Kumar Singh, Preeti Priyam, Gautam Bhowmick

item.title: Cultural Evolution Drives the Emergence of Conventions in Neural Emergent Communication
item.description: arXiv:2611.00006v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent studies of language evolution with neural agents often use models where agents can either speak or listen, where there are only two agents in the population, or where agents can share internal representations. These choices prevent the study of how language emerges through cultural evolution, i.e. through the cumulative adaptation of individual behaviours to fit the communicative needs of the community. We tackle this issue with a new model that trains populations of bi-directional neural agents in a fully distributed fashion to solve a referential game. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on multiple image datasets and show that it is able to scale to large populations. We also show that more conventional languages are easier to learn, providing a direct advantage for cultural transmission. Overall, this work provides a novel approach to neural emergent communication that opens up new directions for evolutionary linguistics.
item.dc:creator: Maxime Toquebiau, J\'er\^ome Botoko Ekila, Paul Van Eecke, Katrien Beuls

item.title: "I Wrote, I Paused, I Rewrote": A Mixed-Methods Study of Learner Perceptions of Process-Aware LLM Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2611.00009v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models increasingly provide formative writing feedback, but most systems evaluate only the submitted text. Process-aware systems can additionally incorporate intermediate drafts and interaction records, yet access to these traces does not establish whether learners perceive the resulting feedback as useful, fair, or aligned with their own revision experience. We conducted a convergent mixed-method post-task evaluation with 43 undergraduate English-language learners. Participants completed a timed essay, received LLM-generated feedback based on the final essay, intermediate snapshots, and keystroke-derived records, and then answered six five-point Likert items and four open-ended questions. Ratings were concentrated above the neutral midpoint across all six items. Between 74.4% and 95.3% of participants selected ratings of 4 or 5, and all six one-sided exact sign tests remained significant after Holm correction. Perceived correspondence between the revision analysis and the participant's reported thought process was positively associated with overall perceived usefulness, Spearman's $\rho_s=.327$, 95% bootstrap CI $[.009,.609]$, $p=.032$, $n=43$. Qualitative responses were analysed through an LLM-assisted codebook development procedure followed by independent human coding of 14 binary codes. Participants frequently described the product feedback and revision rationale as accurate, while a smaller set reported misinterpretation of surface corrections, time constraints, or rhetorical intention. The findings distinguish perceived detection of revision activity from perceived interpretation of why revision occurred.
item.dc:creator: Samra Zafar, Shifa Yousaf

item.title: ARTA: Graph Combinatorial Optimization for Robust Interbeat Interval Estimation from Wearable Electrocardiogram Signals
item.description: arXiv:2611.00011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate heart rate (HR) and interbeat interval (IBI) estimation from wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) is essential for continuous physiological monitoring, but motion artifacts can create false QRS-like peaks and obscure true R-peaks. Conventional detectors and local interval-repair rules process detections independently and may become unreliable when several consecutive beats are corrupted. We present ARTA (Artifact-Robust Temporal Alignment), a graph-based combinatorial framework that estimates the heartbeat sequence through constrained temporal optimization. ARTA combines candidates from multiple ECG detectors, represents them as nodes in a directed acyclic graph and connects candidates through physiologically plausible RR intervals. Candidate confidence uses detector agreement and local ECG quality, while history-dependent transition costs capture recent IBI consistency and a soft heart-rate prior. Beam-search dynamic programming selects a coherent low-cost path across the recording, suppressing false detections and recovering missed beats when plausible auxiliary candidates are available. On the IEEE Signal Processing Cup exercise dataset with electrode-motion artifacts from -2 to 12 dB, ARTA achieved an HR mean absolute error of 1.79 beats per minute, 54% lower than the strongest single-detector baseline, with 92.38% of windows within +/-5 beats per minute, an R-peak F1 score of 0.95, and an IBI mean absolute error of 6.52 ms. Cross-dataset evaluation on the European ST-T Database further assessed transfer to long clinical ambulatory recordings and a label-free reliability analysis examined conditional performance without using reference annotations for segment selection. ARTA is single-channel, training-free, interpretable and computationally lightweight, operating approximately 27 times faster than real time with peak memory below 2.1 MB in a single-thread CPU simulation.
item.dc:creator: Shovito Barua Soumma, Asiful Arefeen, Hassan Ghasemzadeh

item.title: Edge-Optimized YOLOv11n Architecture for Offline Recognition of Nigerian Sign Language Alphanumeric Gestures
item.description: arXiv:2611.00025v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deaf inclusion across sub-Saharan society faces regional hurdles, with Nigeria as the core empirical focus. Existing recognition models demand heavy computational infrastructure. However, standard mobile phones used locally rarely exceed 1 GB to 4 GB of RAM. This study addresses constraints through a lightweight YOLO11n object-detection framework. The system provides real-time Nigerian Sign Language recognition for low-resource hardware. A benchmark dataset containing 11,208 raw gesture images was established. The data spans 33 static classes collected from five signers. Partitioning isolates signers S1 through S3 for training. Signer S4 provides validation data. Signer S5 is reserved for testing. Spatial augmentations are restricted strictly to the training set. This yields 23,509 training images. The validation and test sets each maintain 1,681 images across varied environments. The framework integrates a quantization-aware compression objective. Loss functions merge with squared Frobenius-norm penalties to govern weight distortion. A Spatial-Density Occlusion Index quantifies background complexity and self-occlusion. A latency-profiling equation relates floating-point operations and memory bandwidth to chipset clock speed. Performance testing on physical Android hardware utilizes unquantized FP32 weights. Mean inference latencies span 405.5 ms to 1,759.4 ms. Measured against test data, the algorithm attains a Precision of 0.9975. Recall reaches 0.9991. Mean Average Precision is 0.9942. Outcomes support offline functionality on constrained mobile devices. Practical deployment operates through a mobile utility using CameraX. The application captures gestures in real time. Recognized signs display as text instantly.
item.dc:creator: Adeleke Adeniyan, Abimbola H. Afolayan, Olanrewaju V. Johnson

item.title: A Systematic Analysis of Live Intraoperative Surgical Expert Narrations
item.description: arXiv:2611.00028v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Manual annotation remains the principal bottleneck in surgical video understanding. Live intraoperative narration by the operating surgeon is a scalable alternative that requires no manual annotation, but the information it contains has not been characterized. We analyzed 13 endoscopic lumbar spine decompression procedures (13.2 h) by two senior spine surgeons, using time-synchronized close-mic German audio. An annotation-free pipeline (word-level speech recognition, deterministic correction of surgical-term errors, utterance fusion, LLM-based translation to English, and relevance filtering) converted speech into time-stamped procedural cues labelled with the surgical entities they reference and their speech act. Of 3,171 utterances, 1,201 (37.9%) were retained as procedural cues, while 57.6% were non-procedural and removed. Retained cues referenced instruments (60.7%), anatomy (48.0%) and surgical actions (57.1%), and 98.5% carried at least one of these. 39% of cues (472 of 1,201) were directives, mainly instrument requests and commands. All 467 manually verified instrument requests preceded the instrument's appearance in the field, by a median of 8.2 s. Domain-term transcription corruption affected 18.0% of retained cues. Live narration is thus a dense, annotation-free supervisory signal describing instruments, anatomy, actions and team coordination, but it is noisy and temporally displaced from the events it names, and this displacement must be modelled before safe downstream use.
item.dc:creator: Arda Mamur, Matthias Seibold, Christoph Laux, Florian Wanivenhaus, Philipp F\"urnstahl

item.title: When frequency domain classification is superior to spatial
item.description: arXiv:2611.00073v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern image classification models largely rely on local characteristics and feature extraction for their predictions. This focused approach works well in the spatial domain, but reportedly falls short in the frequency domain, even though both representations contain the same information. This study demonstrates that the significant reduction in accuracy in the frequency domain stems from the lack of local features. Locally swapping data in the frequency domain significantly decreases its inverse spatial domain accuracy, even below that of the frequency domain; however, the frequency domain accuracy remains relatively constant. Moreover, the use of datasets containing global features in the spatial domain yields higher accuracy in the frequency domain. Using these results, a hybrid model is constructed, combining one model trained only in the frequency domain and another trained only in the spatial domain to achieve higher classification accuracy. The proposed visual geometry group (VGG) and vision transformer (ViT) architectures are trained on the ImageNet-100, WikiArt, DTD, FMD, PSVRT, and KTH-TIPS2-b datasets and evaluated.
item.dc:creator: Yanir Harel, Shalom Rosner, Ronit D. Gross, Tal Halevi, Shilo Glam, Ella Koresh, Ido Kanter

item.title: From Zero to OCR: A Data-Centric Framework for Unsupported Low-Resource Scripts
item.description: arXiv:2611.00078v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optical character recognition (OCR) remains inaccessible to many low-resource scripts because annotated document images are unavailable and synthetic training data can fail to preserve script-specific visual structure. We present a data-centric framework that builds end-to-end OCR for such scripts from only an unannotated text corpus and digital fonts, without manually annotating a single training image. A synthetic data engine renders word, line and page images with correct complex-script shaping and automatically derived labels; a YOLOv8 word detector and a convolutional recurrent recognizer trained with connectionist temporal classification learn from these images; and a stage-gate evaluation protocol isolates recognition error before detection is introduced. We demonstrate the framework on Kashmiri, a Perso-Arabic Nastaliq script with approximately 6.8 million speakers that none of six widely used OCR engines supports. Three line-level recognizers, including one transferred from Arabic, stalled between 41% and 79% character error rate (CER), motivating a word-level formulation; subsequent improvements came primarily from rendering fidelity, diacritic-preserving crop margins and tuned non-maximum suppression. The resulting system achieves 0.39% CER on held-out words, 10.0% on synthetic pages and 13.5% on browser-rendered digital pages, and establishes reference results of 18.45% on typeset book pages and 49.8% on degraded historical documents. We publicly release the trained models, the inference code and a synthetic dataset of 285,864 Kashmiri text-line images, and we describe a step-by-step procedure for building OCR for other unsupported scripts.
item.dc:creator: Faizan Iqbal, Haq Nawaz Malik, Hafsah Pervaiz

item.title: HistGramBench: Measuring Structural Recovery When Multimodal Models Redraw Historical Mathematical Diagrams as TikZ
item.description: arXiv:2611.00081v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Digital libraries preserve mathematical books printed from the sixteenth to the twentieth century, but the lettered diagrams in them, the figures on which Euclidean proofs depend, remain scanned images whose content cannot be searched. Redrawing such a diagram as a short drawing program would record which points lie on which lines and circles. But a printed plate offers no source code against which the redrawing could be checked. We introduce HistGramBench, a benchmark of 2,507 diagrams from 95 works printed between 1551 and 1933 in eight languages. For each diagram, two AI models from different providers agree on the facts a reader takes from the figure, such as which lines are parallel or where two lines meet, and every redrawing is checked against those facts on the model's own drawing. We evaluate six affordable AI models. The best recovers about three fifths of these facts, and most of what the models miss comes from programs that never produce a drawing. Parallels and tangencies are the hardest relations to reproduce. HistGramBench gives historians and librarians a way to measure when such tools can make old mathematical diagrams searchable.
item.dc:creator: Minh Quang Tran, Carter He, Cameron Bloch, Zitai Huang, Thien Truong Vo, Trong Nguyen Tran, Isaac Chen

item.title: Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots
item.description: arXiv:2611.00297v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Collaborative robots (cobots) are designed to be safer and more interactive than traditional industrial robots, share the same workspace as humans, and assist them in a range of shop-floor tasks such as palletization, joint assembly, and part inspection. Many of these tasks involve repetitive workflows that may evolve with changes in production environments and task specifications. These requirements motivate the need for intuitive interfaces that allow workers to modify workflows on the shop floor and generalise these routines for future use. This work introduces the Teach-Abstract-Apply (TAA) framework, which enables human operators to (a) teach new workflows to cobots in natural language, (b) abstract the taught workflows into skills for later use, and (c) apply these skills in different settings. As a case study, we apply the TAA framework to a collaborative structure-building task and evaluate it with both open-weight (Qwen3-Coder) and closed (GPT5.2-Codex) models in self-play and cross-model configurations. Our results show that skill abstraction improves task success rates and reduces interaction cost. Beyond automated evaluation, a preliminary human-in-the-loop study suggests that the pipeline also works with human instructions.
item.dc:creator: Chalamalasetti Kranti, Sherzod Hakimov, David Schlangen

item.title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination and Communication in Shared Codebases
item.description: arXiv:2611.00314v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents working in shared repositories may receive separate, independently-motivated requests from human developers, creating a setting that is multi-agent by necessity. When this scenario happens, their individual implementations may work separately but conflict when combined. To study this setting, we introduce ParallACT, a benchmark of orchestrator-free multi-agent coding tasks. ParallACT contains both complementary and contradictory tasks. In complementary tasks, each agent's task is separately useful and implementations must share an interface to be productively combined. In contradictory pairs, both agents' tasks require editing the same code in incompatible ways, and naively combining independent solutions fails to produce a useful implementation. We compare a single-agent oracle given the combined set of tasks against multi-agent settings that vary execution order, visibility, awareness of other agents, and access to a communication channel. We find that the oracle solves most tasks while parallel agents perform substantially worse. Their performance drop is notable for complementary tasks, and particularly sharp for contradictory tasks (e.g., from 62% to 16% for Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8) where merged code typically satisfies only one specification, and the same gap appears in all six further configurations pairing two agent harnesses with three open-weight models. Simply telling an agent that a peer exists does not help significantly, and giving agents access to a communication channel recovers only a small part of the performance, at an additional token cost. ParallACT thus identifies and isolates a core challenge that will become more common as multi-agent coding by independent principals becomes standard, and provides a controlled test of which coordination strategies help, and at what cost.
item.dc:creator: Rishabh Mediratta, Lingyun Xiao, Peter Stone, Joydeep Biswas, Elias Stengel-Eskin

item.title: One Waveform, Two Stories: Benchmarking Speech-Acoustic Conflict in Audio-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.00325v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Audio-language models (ALMs) are evaluated on their understanding of both speech and environmental sounds. What remains underexplored is how they respond when spoken claims contradict acoustic evidence within the same recording. We introduce SAC-Bench, a benchmark of intra-audio speech--acoustic conflict comprising 616,031 unique clips from 188 sound-event classes across seven semantic, temporal, and spatial tasks. It pairs environmental recordings with compatible or contradictory synthesized spoken claims and includes audio-only controls where applicable. Across five open-weight ALMs evaluated on semantic and temporal tasks, high audio-only accuracy often coexists with large losses under conflicting claims; Event Identity accuracy is 24.8--46.5 percentage points lower in conflict than compatible conditions. Temporal Order failures persist even when speech follows the complete event sequence, so simultaneous speech--event masking cannot fully explain them. A spatial case study with Spatial-Omni finds lower motion accuracy associated with both spoken claims and the speech source's physical trajectory. Prompt interventions sometimes restore acoustic accuracy, but can also reduce claim-aligned answers without improving grounding or worsen performance. SAC-Bench thus separates acoustic competence, conflict robustness, and intervention effects.
item.dc:creator: Wenbin Wang, Yuheng Li, Koichiro Yoshino

item.title: SPARK: Self-Correcting Embodied Memory via Physical Re-Observation
item.description: arXiv:2611.00344v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have seen growing adoption in embodied settings as language-queryable memories of the environment. However, existing approaches often assume a reliable single-episode knowledge base (KB) or accumulate observations across episodes without correcting prior errors. Such errors can persist through incorrect semantic labels, inaccurate object positions, and inconsistent spatial relationships. To address this, we present SPARK, a corrective multi-episode framework for embodied RAG. After the first episode, a semantic critic flags regions of the KB, a targeted planner generates revisits, and a selective merge adds, removes, or replaces KB information based on the new observations. We evaluate SPARK on four outdoor AirSim maps under two degraded viewpoint conditions, using perception-built KBs, a visibility-constrained oracle used only for evaluation, and a fixed set of 158 embodied question answering (EQA) questions scored before and after correction. A single corrective episode improves downstream EQA on every map under both conditions while storing 13-41% fewer objects than append-only updating, with gains up to 2.7x on one map-condition pair. Extending correction through Episode 4 brings every map above the EQA performance of its undegraded reference. Ablations show that the critic's three signals each contribute to performance, that targeted revisits achieve a larger mean gain than untargeted ones under the same budget, and that selective merging achieves gains comparable to append-only updating with a smaller KB. Overall, SPARK demonstrates the value of correcting embodied memory through targeted re-observation, particularly as embodied systems scale and the risk of accumulated errors increases.
item.dc:creator: Dmytro Kurdydyk, Aadi Palnitkar, Sebastian Scherer, Seungchan Kim

item.title: Unlearning by Extrapolating a Shrink-and-Heal Lookahead
item.description: arXiv:2611.00374v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Unlearning aims to make a large language model behave like one retrained without its forget set. Prevailing likelihood-suppression objectives, however, lack an explicit forgetting target: they continually reward lower forget-set likelihood, making forgetting sensitive to the optimization budget. We address this limitation by estimating the direction toward the oracle without training it. Our key idea is to shrink the fine-tuned model toward its pre-fine-tuning weights and briefly re-learn the retain set, thereby removing the forget-specific contribution; in the linearized regime, this shrink-and-heal lookahead moves the model a fixed fraction of the way to the retrained model, its unique fixed point. Our method, SHIFT, extrapolates the lookahead's per-token changes into distillation targets and iteratively refines them. Evaluated against eleven baselines under a unified OpenUnlearning protocol, SHIFT achieves the highest aggregate score across all TOFU settings and the closest oracle alignment, 3.7x closer on average than the next-best method; on MUSE, it preserves the most retain knowledge. Under larger optimization budgets, baselines overshoot the oracle, while SHIFT remains near it, even under relearning attacks.
item.dc:creator: Hoang-Chau Luong, Lingwei Chen

item.title: LF-VideoQA: Evaluating Long-Video Understanding with Long-Form Theory-of-Mind Questions
item.description: arXiv:2611.00383v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The hardest part of understanding a long video is not pinpointing any one moment but synthesizing many, e.g., answering a question that requires tracking what develops across hours of content and articulating how the pieces fit together. To date, most long-video QA datasets require only a short answer or a multiple-choice selection, oversimplifying the long-video understanding task to retrieval. We introduce LF-VideoQA, a dataset for long-form, open-ended question answering over long narrative videos built on theory-of-mind questions: a character's belief depends on everything they have seen or been told, so each question demands assembling and reasoning from evidence distributed across the video. The dataset contains more than 6,300 questions on 94 recent films; each requires reasoning over scenes spanning an average of 23 minutes and comes with a question-specific rubric for recall and precision scoring. The dataset is created entirely automatically by annotating screenplays with scene events and each character's first-order beliefs and meta-beliefs, then generating (question, answer, rubric) triples through LLM-based question generation and verification; human studies validate their quality. We evaluate four families of state-of-the-art open-source VLMs across three settings and find the task highly challenging: (i) even an oracle with access to the screenplay falls well short of complete answers; (ii) the best non-oracle model attains barely half of the recall level of the oracle; (iii) unlike on prior long-video benchmarks, captions and subtitles underperform the video itself, indicating that the questions need visual evidence; and (iv) recall is the predominant bottleneck, with answers omitting many required rubric claims.
item.dc:creator: Shaden Shaar, Bradon Thymes, Majd Aldaye, Claire Cardie, Bharath Hariharan

item.title: Geometric and algebraic inference in humans and neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.00387v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Humans possess a remarkable ability to draw inferences from limited data. While some inferences are made intuitively from past experience, others require online reasoning based on novel information given in context. Here, we formalize these strategies, which we term geometric and algebraic inference, and study their computational tradeoffs in humans and neural networks. The geometric strategy gradually shapes representational geometry to reflect underlying relational structure, making subsequent inference cheap. The algebraic strategy flexibly attends to and reasons over novel relations given in context, but costs additional computation at inference time. We identify opposing signatures of these two strategies in transitive inference, a domain widely studied across species, and characterize the conditions under which each is observed. Our framework predicts that the geometric strategy should be dominant when relations are familiar, whereas the algebraic should emerge to support de novo inferences drawn in context. Multiple experiments demonstrate these opposing signatures in humans, neural networks trained from scratch, and large language models (LLMs). Causal interventions in the neural networks reveal that the geometric and algebraic strategies depend on representational geometry and selective attention mechanisms, respectively, and reproduce the effects of analogous neurobiological disruptions in humans. Our framework unifies these effects with disparate phenomena, including content effects observed in human and LLM reasoning and data-distribution effects observed in machine learning. Our findings reconcile competing views of cognitive flexibility that emphasize either representational geometry or algebraic manipulation by showing that each can have unique strengths, and can characterize different aspects of both human and neural network behavior.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Russin, Joonhwa Kim, Ellie Pavlick, Michael J. Frank

item.title: Do Multimodal Models Decide Consistently on Equivalent Optical Spectra?
item.description: arXiv:2611.00428v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A spectrum can be given to a model as a table in nanometers or as a plot in photon energy, and the decision should not depend on which one it sees. When the data needed for an answer are missing, the model should say so. We test representation invariance and abstention on measured optical spectra of silicon metasurfaces (MOCLIP) and gold nanoparticles, with labels computed from the data. Each spectrum is shown as four tables (nm, $\mu$m, scientific notation, eV) and two plots (nm, eV), and partial spectra remove data inside or outside the queried range. We evaluate the decision models d3-nano and Jev 1.13, three GPT-6 Luna configurations and the Qwen3.5-2B base model. Changing only the representation moves accuracy by up to 41 percentage points within one model, mostly on photon-energy tables and plots. With the same evidence, asking in photon energy instead of wavelength helps some model-view pairs by 16-50 points and hurts others by up to 25. When the relevant extremum is removed, unadapted models rarely answer "undetermined". LoRA fine-tuning of d3-nano improves comparisons on the trained table formats, but much of its gain on unanswerable questions comes from a shortcut: it abstains whenever the input is truncated. Training with answerable truncations avoids the shortcut in all six seeds, with a 90-100 point gap between abstention after inside and outside cuts on held-out structures; with the same amount of extra original-task data, five of six seeds keep the shortcut. On gold spectra the two training sets perform similarly. Multimodal language models used for scientific decisions should be tested on equivalent representations and on missing evidence, not only on average accuracy. We release the tasks, per-response results and analysis code.
item.dc:creator: Ziyuan Wang, Genliang Zhu, Xiaobo Chen

item.title: Quantiles, Not Points: Streaming Quantile Matching for Ordinal-Aware LLM-as-a-Judge Calibration
item.description: arXiv:2611.00447v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM-as-a-judge scores are often distributionally shifted from human ratings on any given evaluation task, and post-hoc calibration (mapping LLM to human scores in a small labeled anchor set) has become a popular method to correct for this shift. In this paper we derive the calibration from two positions: that LLMaJ scores are ordinal ratings drawn from a distribution rather than isolated points. We present streaming quantile matching (SQM), a version of a classical method not previously bench marked for LLMaJ calibration, which is built on the two positions by computing the optimal-transport map between the LLM and human score distributions. We develop an evaluation framework and within it we show that unlike point-wise calibrations, SQM respects the ordinality of the human anchor set and achieves the best distributional fidelity and the top overall rank across models and data. We also show that in general, post-hoc calibration narrows the raw error gap between smaller and larger judge models, which opens the possibility of more efficient LLM judges.
item.dc:creator: Ilija Subasic, Andrew Rabinovich, Zhao Chen

item.title: From Small to Large: Assessing Medical Reasoning, Benchmark Contamination, and Model Size in Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.00460v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now answer medical exam questions at or above expert level, but it is unclear whether such scores reflect clinical competence, or are instead affected by the format of the questions being asked (e.g., multiple-choice versus open-ended), prior exposure to the benchmarks, and the difficulty of the questions. These benchmarks are also public and widely used online, which may be resulting in LLM memorization. Models may perform better on questions that they have seen before. It is also not evident whether smaller models, which are more locally deployable in HIPAA-compliant hospital settings, have achieved human performance. In this study, we evaluate fourteen current models from six leading providers, one smaller and one larger model from each provider with two additional open-weight models, on 3,076 questions from four medical benchmarks (MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, and MedBullets) under standard multiple choice, the same questions with the answer choices withheld, and reconstruction of a hidden question from its choices alone. In the standard multiple-choice setting, the strongest models exceed the human-expert baseline on MedQA-USMLE and PubMedQA, but the smaller models trail their larger models by 8.7 percentage points and only two of the six pass the human-expert bar on the licensing examination. Withholding the answer choices, however, makes every model struggle: mean accuracy falls from 82.3% to 50.9%, and the two largest drops belong to the medically specialised models. On memorization, the strongest models reconstruct one question in four from the answer choices alone, yet accuracy holds on the questions they cannot reconstruct. We further weigh accuracy against inference cost and test whether ensembling several models improves medical question answering.
item.dc:creator: Navapat Nananukul, Mayank Kejriwal

item.title: Swap, Replicate, Read the Mass: A Protocol for Auditing Demographic Bias in System One Decision Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.00496v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: System One decision models replace text generation with typed, probability-scored answers and are entering production. Answers execute without a person in the loop, and no multi-model audit exists on established bias benchmarks. We provide that audit: three benchmarks: BBQ (all eleven categories), CrowS-Pairs, and SilverSpoon, adapted to the typed interface, twelve models plus a no-thinking ablation, and 1,638,000 decisions. Every order-sensitive item runs twice with options swapped; native typed models also swap labels; ten configurations repeat under extra seeds and batch 16. We find widespread stereotype alignment, order-dependent answers, and confidence that tracks instability rather than bias. In BBQ, 97 of 143 model-by-category scores are significant and 94 aligned, while the commercial reference abstains on 99.5% of ambiguous items, hiding aligned probability mass. Option swaps flip 0.0% to 72.6% of choices; typed scoring stays below 10% except Laya (22-33%), and untuned letter prompting reaches 73%. CrowS-Pairs preference spans 0.496 to 0.816, and boolean answers can be decided by position (1.00 versus 0.005). SilverSpoon judgments shift toward lower-SES labels in five of eight decision models, inherited from the 9B backbone or induced by tuning. Audits must permute options and reverse questions by default; order-invariant scoring should become a procurement requirement.
item.dc:creator: Alejandro Mozo Quesada (Universidad de M\'alaga, Spain), Sergio G\'alvez Rojas (Universidad de M\'alaga, Spain), Francisco L\'opez Valverde (Universidad de M\'alaga, Spain)

item.title: Robustness Starts with the Objective: Designing and Certifying Robust LLM-Generated Heuristics
item.description: arXiv:2611.00504v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLMs are increasingly used to design heuristics for computer systems. However, most synthesis frameworks evaluate candidates by their average performance, which can mask severe regressions on specific workloads. Even adding adversarial training inputs doesn't eliminate these regressions, and percentile objectives (e.g., optimizing for the 95th percentile) overlook how severe regressions can be beyond the selected threshold. We present TAILOR, a framework that guides LLM synthesis using the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) of the cost difference between each candidate and an existing baseline on the same workload. This paired CVaR measures the average difference over the worst fraction of workloads. We show that a negative paired CVaR guarantees improvements in both average performance and tail optimality gap relative to the unknown optimum, without ever computing that optimum. We find that TAILOR achieves the best mean--tail trade-off among the synthesis objectives we evaluate across three case studies: Azure GPU batch admission, Azure VM packing, and server placement. Tested across seven diverse optimization benchmarks, TAILOR produces heuristics that are certified with 99% confidence to improve both average performance and tail optimality gaps over the baseline in six of them. On these six benchmarks, TAILOR also outperforms known robust, human-designed alternatives in the tail while achieving better or comparable average-performance improvement over the baseline.
item.dc:creator: Pantea Karimi, Roozbeh Bostandoost, Dany Rouhana, Siva Kesava Reddy Kakarla, Pooria Namyar, Mohammad Alizadeh, Venkat Arun, Behnaz Arzani

item.title: Agentic Context Management for Multi-Turn Human-AI Conversations
item.description: arXiv:2611.00518v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLMs degrade in multi-turn conversation partly because of context pollution: the model's own earlier outputs stay in context and anchor later turns, so an early misreading of the user's intent can persist after the user corrects it. Assistant omission (AO), dropping every assistant message, removes this pollution but fails when interaction is referential: later turns refer back to drafts, decisions, and tool-call results that exist only in assistant turns. We propose Agentic Conversation Context Curation (AC3), a training-free method in which a separate analyzer (1) consolidates the task specification from the user's messages alone, (2) audits the assistant's prior outputs against it, and (3) edits the context, either appending the analysis or discarding the assistant side and rebuilding the context from the specification. A second finding: pollution is contagious. An analyzer that sees the assistant's reasoning while extracting the specification can do worse than no intervention, and instructing it to ignore them did not close the gap, so we exclude assistant turns structurally. On Lost in Conversation (replaying difficulty-selected instances), where AO is an oracle by construction, AC3 closes 55-84% of the gap between full context and AO on three of four tasks and exceeds AO on the fourth, and an LLM that faithfully summarizes the history does not reproduce the gain even with more compute. On real WildChat conversations, a GPT-5-mini judge prefers AC3's next turn over both full context and AO in every configuration of our main table, though this preference depends on the judge; on CollabLLM results are mixed. In stateful tool use (tau2-bench), AO collapses to 0% on every model; AC3 does not collapse, though it falls slightly behind full context. Detector studies show that Reset removes injected pollution but is not span-selective: the gain comes from rebuilding the specification.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Ho, Chenglong Wang, Baolin Peng, Nebojsa Jojic, Philippe Laban, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao, Lianhui Qin

item.title: WeSearch: A Unified Model-Centric Retrieval Framework for WeChat Search
item.description: arXiv:2611.00530v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present WeSearch, a unified, model-centric retrieval framework for large-scale, continuously evolving content search. Prevailing methods assign documents fixed hierarchical Semantic IDs, implicitly assuming each document follows a single coherent semantic path-an assumption that often breaks down for multi-topic documents. WeSearch instead retrieves query-relevant clusters and then ranks atomic documents within the resulting query-specific candidate space, decoupling candidate pruning from fine-grained relevance modeling. Combined with relevance-aware training, compact document representations, and incremental index updates, this design enables weekly-or daily when needed-model refreshes. Deployed as the primary semantic retrieval path in WeChat Search alongside a lexical syntax tree, WeSearch shows consistent one-week A/B gains on corpora from hundreds of millions to billions of documents, and a one-month full-traffic A/B test confirms stable improvements of +0.68% CTR and +2.27% per-user article clicks, together with a 41% reduction in retrieval resource cost and a 19 ms reduction in graphic-text retrieval latency. WeSearch is now fully deployed in WeChat Search, serving 100% of production traffic.
item.dc:creator: Kepu Zhang, Yuzhe Cai, Yue Shu, Dawei Chen, Jinhai Zhu, Yuan Xu, Zehua Dai, Tongke Ni, Ziyao Chen, Chen Fu, Jie Shao, Chao Wang, Xiangmin Wang, Ruifeng Zhao, Rongchun Yao, Jie Yin, Weixin Qiu, Nan Song, Junyang Li, Fan Li, Quanchao Hui, Yulong Ou, Qiang Chen, Hao Cao, Sen Yang

item.title: Skill++: Towards Lifelong Agents via Routing-Aware Skill Refinement
item.description: arXiv:2611.00544v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents extend their capabilities with skills, each with a name, a description, and a body. Under progressive disclosure, an LLM router selects skills by name and description alone and loads only the selected bodies. Skill libraries grow continually as users and agents add new skills. Because the router relies on this metadata, a similar new skill can displace an earlier one, breaking previously correct routing even though the earlier skill and the router are unchanged. This routing interference is aggravated for public skills, whose descriptions may not match their bodies. We formulate the problem as lifelong skill routing, a class-incremental continual learning problem. A solution must keep earlier skills selectable without suppressing new ones. Existing approaches fall short, since continually retraining the router risks catastrophic forgetting and rewriting methods either ignore similar skills or require per-skill feedback. We therefore propose Skill++, which rewrites only the name and description of each incoming skill, without router training or labeled data. The new description states what the body supports, how the skill differs from its closest predecessor, and what related work it excludes. As a library grows to 731 skills over ten sessions, Skill++ selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries, versus 36.4% under the original metadata. Across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, it outperforms all compared approaches, and its gains carry over to the Codex CLI agent harness.
item.dc:creator: Hanrong Zhang, Minghao Liang, Jiawei Wu, Yankai Chen, Shicheng Fan, Zhiwei Liu, Enze Ma, Junwei Yuan, Tianyi Wang, Dehai Min, Kening Zheng, Xue Liu, Philip S. Yu

item.title: Conic Certification of Transformer Attention
item.description: arXiv:2611.00585v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Attention is the computational core of large language models, yet the verifiers that bound how far an attention head's output can move under input perturbations give no guarantee on how loose their bounds are. A weak certificate therefore cannot be told apart from a fragile model. We develop a conic programming theory of attention certification that supplies this guarantee. We prove that the difficulty lies not in the softmax but in the bilinear interaction of a varying query with the keys. This interaction makes certification NP-hard over boxes and inapproximable once the attention logits can move by a constant amount. A fixed query or listed token substitutions, by contrast, make the exact worst case efficiently computable. An exponential cone moment relaxation then certifies a head with an error bounded quadratically in the perturbation radius by computable quantities, an order that cannot be improved. We also show that relaxations that treat a network one operation at a time, linear bound propagation among them, pay on second-order terms a sum of per-operation maxima instead of one coupled maximum. Computational results on GPT-2 indicate that the theory carries over to a trained model. Against exact worst cases with the query fixed, the certificate attains the predicted second-order accuracy. It is tighter than linear bound propagation on every head, and the looseness of bound propagation tracks the predicted per-operation excess.
item.dc:creator: Masoud Ataei

item.title: TVP: TV is Almost All You Need for Speculative Decoding
item.description: arXiv:2611.00588v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference with a drafter whose proposed tokens are verified by the target model in parallel. Under lossless speculative sampling, a draft token is accepted with probability one minus the total variation (TV) distance between the target and draft distributions, yet drafters are often trained with cross-entropy (CE) or KL. We first show that under matched and well-tuned training, TV matches or surpasses several published draft-training objectives when fine-tuning, and a fixed TV and KL mixture does the same when training from scratch. We identify two remaining problems, TV's vanishing gradients on undercovered tokens and the prefix products that starve later positions in acceptance-length objectives. To address both, we derive TVP, a loss family based on expected acceptance length, whose power parameter interpolates between coverage and acceptance oriented objectives. Annealing the power from zero to one gives the highest or tied-highest acceptance length across three drafter architectures and three target models, including longer drafts and block verification. TVP improves acceptance length over CE by 9.8% when fine-tuning, and over the public DFlash2 training recipes by 6.2 to 12.9%.
item.dc:creator: Aaryam Sharma

item.title: Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin
item.description: arXiv:2611.00606v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Attribution graphs over the features of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used to predict what an ablation does and are compared across training seeds. A TopK SAE keeps the largest preactivations at each token, and a feature's margin is its preactivation's distance to the cutoff. On five public TopK SAE pairs from three Pythia models, zeroing one feature moves a next layer feature across the cutoff in 0.74 of cases or more, and the crossings carry most of the response's energy. Over writes that scale a feature's code by three factors, the graph built on the features active beforehand has a median relative error of 0.247 or more. The margin graph adds the first order change to every preactivation and reranks, at the same cost, and errs by at most 0.033. At the median, the crossing features' decoded change is 1.24 times the model's own change in norm or more. Between seeds of one testbed, sparse maps between features explain 0.85 of a graph's energy on its active features, and 0.47 once the other seed's graph keeps only its own. The largest model studied is pythia-160m.
item.dc:creator: Karl Li

item.title: Heirloom: Carrying a Phone's Personalization Across Base-Model Generations
item.description: arXiv:2611.00650v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: On-device language models can learn a user's preferences through adapters trained on private data. However, a base-model upgrade may change the layers or vocabulary, leaving the personal adapter incompatible. Replacing it with a non-personal adapter loses much of the personalization, while retraining requires retaining the user's labeled history. We present Heirloom, a system that transfers a personal adapter to a new base model on the phone without retaining labels. Heirloom uses the old personal model as a teacher, collecting its predictions on stored unlabeled inputs, vendor-provided prompts, or prompts generated by the new base. It then unloads the old base and trains an adapter for the new model to match those predictions, keeping only one base model in memory at a time. We evaluate Heirloom across three generation upgrades from two model families, an architecture-preserving refresh, and three personalization tasks. On movie tagging, migration from stored inputs maintains pre-upgrade accuracy and differs from labeled retraining by at most 1.7 percentage points across the three upgrades. On a phone's neural processing unit (NPU), a fixed-length migration for the 4B upgrade takes 38 minutes and consumes 20% of the battery end to end, making the stored-input setting feasible during overnight charging.
item.dc:creator: Zhuomin Chen, Jingchao Ni, Qingkai Dong, Xu Zheng, Gabriel H\"ubner Lucchesi, Mo Sha, Wei Cheng, Dongsheng Luo

item.title: Learning Timeline-Preserving Speech-to-Speech Translation
item.description: arXiv:2611.00690v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) increasingly preserves what is said and how it sounds, but not necessarily when speech and silence occur. For dubbing and other temporally grounded applications, matching total duration is not enough: speech and pauses must also occur at corresponding moments. We formulate timeline-preserving S2ST, which aims to preserve the source endpoint and salient internal pauses on a shared absolute timeline. We present TransDubber, an end-to-end autoregressive system that learns this temporal structure directly from aligned target waveforms, without inference-time frame-level timing control or post-hoc temporal correction. To provide this supervision, we construct 642K exactly duration-matched English-Chinese speech pairs by translating and synthesizing target speech on source-defined temporal scaffolds. Training combines a progressive supervised curriculum with verifier-guided reinforcement learning to balance translation quality and temporal alignment. On a 4,353-utterance test set spanning read and spontaneous speech, TransDubber increases the proportion of translations within 2% of the source duration from 25.6% to 61.5% and pause-alignment F1 from 0.118 to 0.550 compared with UniSS, while maintaining competitive translation quality. Our analysis shows that aligned supervision establishes timeline following, while reinforcement learning refines temporal precision and partially offsets the translation-quality cost of strict synchronization. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of our data and training framework for timeline-preserving S2ST. Audio samples, code, datasets, and pretrained models are available at https://zhishengzheng.com/transdubber/.
item.dc:creator: Zhisheng Zheng, David Harwath

item.title: ConstraintMatch: Compositional Image-Text Matching through Constrained Regional Evidence Selection
item.description: arXiv:2611.00784v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Local image--text matching can find strong evidence for individual concepts yet favor captions with incorrect attribute--entity bindings. We introduce ConstraintMatch, a training-free inference method that turns entity-level regional consistency into an explicit matching cost. On the same frozen condition--region similarity matrix, it compares independent crop selection for each category and attribute with a shared crop choice within each entity. Their gap quantifies the score advantage obtained by relaxing the shared-region constraint. Spatial references from the same image calibrate this gap by keeping category evidence fixed while jointly shifting an entity's attribute maps. Per-entity clipping prevents cancellation across residuals, and the scaled mean cost is subtracted from global similarity. ConstraintMatch uses pooled embeddings, and spatial calibration requires no additional encoder calls. With parameters fixed per backbone across tasks, ConstraintMatch improves over global matching by 7.70 percentage points on full ARO Attribute and 5.63 points on held-out SugarCrepe++ attribute swaps, averaged across Qwen~2B and CORE~2B. Against SGI adapted to the same 13-crop budget, the respective gains are 4.85 and 3.51 points. Controlled analyses distinguish the effects of shared-region matching and candidate score calibration. The results establish entity-level evidence selection as a practical scoring principle for compositional multimodal retrieval.
item.dc:creator: Yuhong Zhou, Yubo Gao, Xiangbo Shu

item.title: ODC: Orthogonal Drift Correction for Improved Text-to-Image Semantic Alignment at Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.00819v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Text-to-image models have achieved remarkable success in generating high-quality images from textual descriptions. However, they often struggle with "semantic drift," where the generated output fails to precisely align with complex or nuanced text prompts. While recent approaches have attempted to address semantic errors regarding attribute binding or object presence, there remains a gap for a more holistic method that addresses these issues by directly refining the text embeddings of the initial user prompt. In this work, we introduce Orthogonal Drift Correction (ODC), an inference-time guidance method designed to mitigate semantic drift without requiring model retraining or additional user inputs. ODC guides image generation through a two-stage process. In the first stage, it identifies the semantic drift by evaluating the initially generated image against the user prompt in a shared vision-language embedding space. It then isolates the component of this drift vector that is orthogonal to the prompt's direction and translates it back into text via a vocabulary-based surrogate mechanism. In the second stage, it produces refined text conditioning for a second generation pass by feeding both the initial text embedding and the re-embedded drift representation into an adaptive rank-reduced concept removal module. Our experiments demonstrate that ODC consistently improves prompt-image alignment, increasing CLIP scores by up to 5.4% over the baseline on the COALBench-300 and PartiPrompts benchmarks. Furthermore, on the T2I-CompBench complex subset, ODC improves the average 3-in-1 score by 4.5% over the competing methods. As a plug-and-play module, ODC offers a practical and efficient method for improving the reliability of text-to-image models. Code is available at https://github.com/kasrakamali/ODC.
item.dc:creator: Kasra Kamali, Basim Azam, Tuan Duong Trinh, Jean Honorio, Naveed Akhtar

item.title: Fewer Tokens, More Answers: Verifiable-Reward Tuning of an Ornith-Style VLM for Multi-View Driving QA
item.description: arXiv:2611.00833v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reasoning-enabled model derivatives must turn intermediate deliberation into a usable answer within a deployment budget. We study that transition in an Ornith checkpoint adapted to multi-camera driving question answering with verifiable rewards. Paired archived outputs show that, on a selected 400-question development screen with a 256-token cap, GRPO increases answer extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%. Of 39 wrong-to-correct transitions, 33 begin with an unextractable base response. The base's 87 unextractable responses all reach the token cap. Checkpoint-verified reconstruction on those same questions gives a much smaller first-pass accuracy gain at 512 tokens: +0.75 percentage points, versus +8.25 at 256. A later answer-cued continuation is analyzed separately; it helps the base more and narrows the adapter difference. On the full 2,511-question development set, this recovery-enabled pipeline reduces mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain. We frame these findings as adaptation of answer delivery under finite budgets, with explicit selection and provenance limits. Ornith's self-scaffolding lineage and newer reasoning-enabled derivatives such as Bonsai motivate the problem, but our measured results concern Ornith alone and do not establish a shared architectural mechanism or cross-model transfer.
item.dc:creator: T N Rickesh, Pranav Vinodh, Sowmya Kamath S

item.title: When 200 OK Is Not an Answer: Silent Fetch Failures in Agentic Web Content Acquisition
item.description: arXiv:2611.00884v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Web agents and answer engines fetch pages at question time, and liveness checks of cited sources treat an HTTP 200 response as success. We measure how often that assumption fails and what it does to measurements built on fetched pages. We fetched 10,307 URLs in three days with a polite static client and a rendered browser client: pages from 1,507 sites in five strata, random non-existent paths on every site, and the 4,795 URLs cited by expert-verified claims in ExpertQA. We define a taxonomy of what a 200 response contains, label the static 200 responses automatically, and check the labels against 300 items reviewed by an LLM-based assistant; a human check of 60 of them retained every reviewed usability label after discussion. By the automatic labels, 20.9% of the pages that a static client receives with status 200 do not contain the page's main content: app shells, bot challenges, block pages, error and placeholder pages, and partial content. On the held-out test split, the reviewed sample lowers this estimate from 25.5% to 20.0%. 13.1% of the sites whose random-path probe was answered returned 200. The error propagates: for the cited sources, treating 200 as content overstates the share of claim-source pairs that can be checked against live content by 12.2 points and inflates the apparent silent citation-drift rate from 5.8% to 21.9%. Cheap heuristics catch most of it. Text length, probe comparison and redirect-to-root, combined and tuned on held-out sites, recover 86% of unusable reviewed responses at a false-alarm rate near 5%. Content-reading detectors perform comparably: the best, the text classifier, gains five to seven points of recall at more than twice the false-alarm rate. We argue that agents and their evaluations should report fetch outcomes explicitly instead of inferring them from the status line and will release the labelled data and code.
item.dc:creator: Shuyang Zhang (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)

item.title: Multi-Turn Semantic Caching for Low-Cost LLM Serving
item.description: arXiv:2611.01077v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semantic caching lowers the cost of serving large language models (LLMs) by reusing stored responses for similar requests. In multi-turn conversations, whether a cached response is acceptable depends on both conversations' histories, which embedding similarity of requests and histories predicts poorly (AUC 0.62--0.74 on five workloads). We therefore learn the \emph{reuse risk}, the probability that a cached response is unacceptable, from judge feedback, and choose a budgeted set of conversation states to cache by weighing the generation cost a reuse avoids against a price for unacceptable reuse. We propose CUCB-SC-MT, which learns a cache from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, and CLCB-LS-MT, which learns online and has $\tilde O(\sqrt N)$ regret over $N$ requests when conversation states recur. On math-tutoring (SocraTeach) and movie-ticketing (Taskmaster-3) conversations, both achieve lower loss than prior semantic caching approaches: ContextCache, multi-turn variants of ElastiCache and vCache, and single-turn semantic caching at every cache budget. With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35--41\% of the generation cost through acceptable reuses, against at most 22--25\% for the baselines, and lowers estimated serving latency by 19--35\%.
item.dc:creator: Baran Atalar, Selly Beyene, Xutong Liu, Carlee Joe-Wong

item.title: Concept-Guided Prompting Strategies Increase Diversity in LLM-Generated Recipe Populations
item.description: arXiv:2611.01171v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Novelty in solution generation supports automated discovery, but LLM outputs can remain repetitive. To address this, we propose a simple concept-guided prompting method that generates thematic concepts before responses within each of these concepts. To demonstrate, we generated 1,000 recipes for a recipe book task and compared the results against a human-authored corpus. Two naive prompting strategies were compared as baselines. Concept-guided prompting outperformed both baselines in all cases and reached semantic coverage of 47.0% versus 35.1% and 13.1% in respective prior-title and nonce prompt strategies. These findings suggest broader population exploration and diversity, but remain contained to this specific task. Further work is needed to determine the quality of solutions and generalizability.
item.dc:creator: Stuart Farmer

item.title: Does Random Search Discover Task Experts? Revisiting Neural Thickets
item.description: arXiv:2611.01262v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pretrained models are typically viewed as generalists, requiring bespoke post-training to achieve task-specific expertise. Gan & Isola (2026) recently proposed a striking alternative: that pretrained models lie in a dense neural thicket of task specialists, which can be surfaced with simple Gaussian weight perturbations. We examine this neural thicket of task-specific experts and identify several key findings that question this perspective. First, we find that the apparent lift of the best-of-N selected perturbation decays quickly with selection-set size m, strongly suggesting overfitting to the selection questions. In fact, for 10 of the 12 model-task pairs we study, a simple null model of pure selection noise predicts more than 75 percent of the top expert's reward lift. Second, the top experts' advantage often vanishes on held-out questions or remains within the run-to-run variability of the unperturbed pretrained model. Third, we find that majority voting over the top-K selected perturbations, termed RandOpt(N, K) by Gan & Isola (2026), is often matched or outperformed by majority voting over K samples from the base model. Overall, our results suggest that random weight perturbations may be ineffective at uncovering task experts around pretrained models, and that task adaptation requires more sophistication than random search. Code and artifacts are available at github.com/asil012/RevisitingNeuralThickets.
item.dc:creator: Julian Asilis, Guanzhe Hong, Vatsal Sharan

item.title: Geometry of Confabulation and Refusal in Small Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.01272v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Faced with an unanswerable question, small language models can either refuse or confabulate: confidently produce a wrong answer. Can the hidden state before the first generated token provide a clue? Can we flip confabulations into refusals?
